1:
Who wrote the letter is less settled than almost anything else in the New Testament, and Clarke says so: there have been more doubts and more diversity of opinion about the author and date of this epistle than about most other parts of the canon. Two men of the name appear in the Gospels, the son of Zebedee and the son of Alpheus called the Lord's brother; Michaelis leans to the first, while other great authorities give it to the second, the president of the church at Jerusalem. Clarke then lists four senses in which that man could be called a brother of the Lord: a child of Joseph by an earlier marriage; a child of Joseph and Mary born after the Lord's birth, which he thinks extremely probable; a son raised up to a brother of Joseph who died childless, which he thinks unlikely, since one son would then have sufficed where four are named; or a cousin, the Hebrews commonly calling cousins brethren. Henry fastens on what the writer does not claim. Though a prime minister in Christ's kingdom he styles himself only a servant, from which Henry draws the rule that those highest in office in the church are but servants and should act as ministers and not masters; and though the evangelist calls him the Lord's brother, it was his glory to serve Christ in the spirit rather than boast of kinship according to the flesh. Robertson presses it harder: the writer calls himself not brother but bondservant, and sets God and the Lord Jesus Christ on a level, so that James is no Ebionite but accepts the deity of his own brother, difficult as that must have been.

The people addressed are named by an old formula. Ellicott renders it the twelve tribes in the dispersion and grants that the number is in part figurative, since by then Judah and Benjamin had largely returned while the ten had lost their tribal distinctions and vanished from record. He notes that long before the fall of Jerusalem Jewish colonists were settled through Europe as well as Asia. Calvin gives the same history more briefly, that the ten tribes were placed by the Assyrian king in various parts and afterwards moved in all directions as kingdoms revolved, so that James wrote to exhort those he could not address in person; and he distinguishes the earlier dispersion under the Assyrian captivity from the later one under the Greek power, thinking that a letter written in Greek was meant especially for the second. Wesley takes the address to mean those of the tribes that believe, ten having been scattered since the reign of Hoshea and much of the rest now dispersed through the Roman empire, as Moses had foretold.

The salutation itself is a single word. Gill explains the title of servant as meaning more than the service every creature owes or every regenerate man renders, since it is here an office: the writer served God in the gospel of his Son and was an apostle, other apostles styling themselves the same way. Robertson observes that the infinitive of greeting is the ordinary idiom of the papyrus letters, and occurs in no other New Testament epistle, though it stands at the head of the letter sent from Jerusalem to Antioch. He adds that the Jews of that period fell roughly into Palestinian agriculturists speaking Aramaic and city-dwelling traders of the Dispersion speaking Greek. Henry reads the greeting as respect for men in hard circumstances, since true Christians should not be the less valued for their hardships, and it was the desire of the writer's heart that the scattered might be comforted and rejoice even in their distresses. Barnes surveys what follows and divides it in two: temptation and trial, complete within this chapter, and the nature of true religion, begun here and carried into the next.
2:
The word rendered temptations has to be rescued before the sentence can be read. Barnes points out that it now commonly means placing an allurement before a man to induce him to sin, and is so used later in the chapter, but that here it means trials — persecution, poverty, calamity of any kind. Such things are not inducements to sin; they test faith and show whether the man tried will hold to God or fall away, coinciding with temptation properly so called only in putting religion to the proof. Clarke says the same shortly, that the word signifies affliction, persecution or trial of any kind and does not here intend diabolical suggestion. Robertson traces the drift in English: the word is Latin and originally covered trials whether good or bad, but the evil sense has monopolised it, though we still say attempt. He adds that trials rightly faced are harmless while trials wrongly met become temptations to evil, and glosses the adjective, as old as Homer, to mean variegated or many-coloured.

That such things should be counted joy is a bold demand, and Calvin explains why it was needed. The very name of the nation was so infamous that these readers were hated wherever they went, and their Christian profession made them more miserable still, setting their own countrymen against them as their bitterest enemies. He takes the word to cover all adverse things, so called because they test our obedience, and finds a reason for their variety: trials mortify the flesh, and since its vices continually shoot up they must be often repeated, while ambition, avarice, envy, gluttony and the lusts we abound in cannot be cured by one medicine. To count it joy is to reckon trials gain. Yet Calvin will not pretend the grief away, since all our senses are so formed that every trial produces sorrow and no man can divest himself of his nature — which does not prevent the children of God from rising by the Spirit above the sorrow of the flesh. Henry sets the contrast against the schools: philosophy may instruct men to be calm under their troubles, but Christianity teaches them to be joyful, since these exercises proceed from love and not fury in God. He notes that the afflictions are such as a good man does not create for himself but falls into, and that the gold is put in the furnace to be purified. Wesley adds that this joy is the highest degree of patience, containing all the rest.

How a frail creature is to obey is the last question, and two voices meet it from the Lord's prayer. Ellicott asks how men who pray to be led not into temptation can rejoice in it, and answers from the nature of grace, which grows by use as the powers of body and mind do and decays when unemployed: a veteran who has proved his armour is worth more than a raw recruit, and innocence stands below the purity won by long conflict. Temptation, he insists, is not sin — you cannot prevent the birds from flying over your head, as the old divine said, but you can prevent their nesting in your hair — and the petition asks help in the trial rather than escape from it. Cyril puts the same solution as a question about words: since a man untempted is unproved, and James bids us count it joy, entering into temptation must mean being overwhelmed by it. Temptation is like a winter torrent hard to cross, and those not swept away pass through as good swimmers. Judas entered the temptation of the love of money and drowned; Peter entered the temptation of the denial and swam through. Gill notes that the men addressed are brethren not merely as fellow Jews but as men born again of the same grace, of one household of faith.
3:
The noun rendered trying has been fixed by the papyri, and Robertson reports the gain: the word is known as an adjective meaning standard or approved, as of gold, so that the phrase means the genuine element in your faith rather than the crucible or the process — faith stands the test of fire and is passed as sterling. The patience it produces he glosses as staying power, the old word for remaining under a load. Clarke describes the same process from the man's side: trials put religion and all its graces to proof, and one who stands in them gives evidence that his religion is sound, the evidence to his own mind inducing him to take courage and persevere. Barnes adds that patience is worth whatever the trial costs to procure it, and notices something about the writer: this is one of the passages showing that James knew Paul's writings, the sentiment being found in the fifth of Romans — though Paul carries it further, tracing other effects of tribulation, while James asks only that patience have its perfect work.

Calvin takes up the objection the command invites, how it comes that we judge that sweet which to the sense is bitter, and answers from the effect: we dread disease and want and exile and prison and reproach and death because we regard them as evils, but when we learn that God's kindness turns them into helps toward our salvation, it is ingratitude to murmur instead of submitting to such fatherly dealing. He then sets James beside Paul and finds an apparent contradiction, since Paul makes probation the third thing, produced by patience, where James puts it first as the cause. The solution he gives is that the same word bears an active sense in one and a passive in the other: James means the act of testing, which produces patience, while Paul means the experience gained by enduring, from which hope grows. He adds a caution against reading either as natural law, since the minds of men are not so formed that affliction of itself breeds patience — the ungodly are provoked by it to madness, as Pharaoh proves — and what both apostles regard is the providence of God through which the faithful learn it. Gill notes that this is known by experience, as everyone trained in the school of affliction knows it, and Ellicott that the verse confirms what went before, the habit of patience being the blessed result of all the weary effort under God's probation, which James himself had learned long and painfully.

What the perfect work amounts to is then defined. Clarke explains the noun as any effect produced by a cause, like interest from money or fruit from tillage, so that the perfect work is the full reward; and he takes the two adjectives that follow as fully instructed in every part of the doctrine of God, and as having all one's parts and members, so that knowledge and holiness bear a proper proportion to each other. Some think both terms borrowed from the Grecian games, the victor being called perfect and the winner of the five exercises entire; Clarke prefers to find them in the sacrifices, where a victim was perfect if sound and free of disease, and entire if it had all its members, nothing redundant and nothing deficient. Barnes reads the imperative as a warning against interference: let patience be fairly developed and not obstructed by murmuring, complaint or rebellion, since a man may have the elements of a good character and sound principles which are never carried out far enough to show what they are, and afflictions more than anything else will do it. Wesley gives the whole in three strokes — give patience full scope under whatever trials befall you, be adorned with every Christian grace, and want nothing that God requires in you.
5:
Which wisdom is meant is settled first. Barnes takes it to be chiefly the kind needed in trials — wisdom to understand their design, to do the duties that grow out of them, and to find out the sins for which the affliction came — though the language is general enough to cover every want, since we are in great danger of going wrong when afflicted, and so of losing the benefit we might have had. Clarke distinguishes the ordinary sense from the biblical: wisdom generally means knowing the best end and the best means of reaching it, but in Scripture it stands for true religion, the practical knowledge of God, of oneself and of a Saviour. He adds the Greek maxim that looks strange and is literally true, that the knowledge of ignorance is the beginning of knowledge. Gill draws an inference from the supposition itself: the perfection spoken of just before cannot be meant of this life, since the writer immediately assumes that his readers lack wisdom — and the wisdom wanted is to see God as the author of affliction rather than charge it to chance or second causes, as Job did not ascribe his calamities to the Chaldeans or the wind or Satan, but to God.

The command to ask is examined closely on both sides. Robertson notes a banking figure in the verb, to be short of wisdom — not of knowledge but of wisdom, the practical use of knowledge — and reads the imperative as let him keep on asking, the promise that follows echoing the words of Jesus. Barnes urges that the particular case be brought before God, since it is a privilege of Christians not merely to ask the general wisdom needed for life but to bring each perplexity to the throne; and he observes that the word men in the next clause was supplied by the translators, the promise being restricted to those who ask. In Scripture, he says, the promise of divine aid is always limited to the desire: no blessing is promised to a man who does not value it enough to pray. Calvin explains why the command comes here, since our reason and all our feelings are averse to the thought that we can be happy in the midst of evils; and he draws a rule from it, that whenever God commands anything we should ask from him the power to perform it. To the question why the writer says if any, as though not all lacked wisdom, he answers that all are by nature without it, but some have been given the spirit of wisdom and others not — and that asking an increase is a different thing from asking for it at first.

The two words describing the Giver are dwelt on longest. Ellicott would change liberally to simply, since the point is that God gives fully and directly and does not reproach the man who asks; and he sets the contrast with human generosity by quoting Dante in exile, who learned how salt is another man's bread, and the son of Sirach, who says the fool gives little and upbraids much. Calvin takes the word for promptitude in giving: God is so ready that he rejects none and puts none haughtily off, unlike the niggardly who give sparingly as with a closed hand, or give part of what they meant, or debate long whether to give at all. The second word he thinks added lest anyone fear to come too often, since the most open-handed of men, asked repeatedly, recite their former kindnesses by way of excuse, so that we are ashamed to weary them — whereas God is ready always to add new blessings to the old, without end. Wesley states both halves in a line: God gives to all who ask aright, and upbraids them neither with past wickedness nor present unworthiness.
6:
The condition attached to the promise is faith, and Calvin sets out what that means in prayer. We cannot pray without the word leading the way, so we must believe before we pray, since by praying we testify that we hope to obtain the grace God has promised — and a man with no faith in the promises prays dissemblingly. Faith, then, is what relies on those promises and makes us sure of obtaining, so that it is bound up with confidence and certainty about God's love toward us. Gill gives the same content in list form: faith not only that God is, but in the promises he has made, in his power and faithfulness to perform them, and that whatever is asked according to his will shall be given. Clarke adds a sentence that turns the requirement into an encouragement, that no man can believe too much good of God. Ellicott observes that this verse alone would clear the writer of the charge of slighting faith, since he puts it here in the very forefront of necessity, without which all prayer is useless.

What the opposite state is gets closer attention. Robertson explains the participle from a verb meaning to separate between, to discriminate, and notes that no example of it in the sense of being divided against oneself has been found earlier than the New Testament — it is a vivid picture of internal doubt. Ellicott defines the same thing as a halting between belief and unbelief with the inclination toward the latter, and answers the question it raises, how an unhesitating faith is to be got: faith is the direct gift of God, but it must be tended and used or its faculties are soon gone, and the shield of faith quenches the fiery darts only when it is lifted up in an act of faith. He adds a distinction worth keeping, that intellectual doubt is not moral doubt and the unorthodox are not as the adulterous — though intellectual doubt may itself spring from a habit of carping criticism and self-opinion, for which a man is answerable. Calvin turns the verse against a settled teaching: it disproves the dogma held as an oracle throughout the Papacy, that we ought to pray doubtingly and uncertain of success, since prayers are not heard except where there is confidence of obtaining. He allows that through the infirmity of the flesh nobody escapes being shaken, but temptations of that kind are overcome by faith at last, as a tree with firm roots shakes in the wind without being rooted up.

The simile itself is examined word by word. Robertson identifies the noun as a dashing or surging wave rather than the successive rollers, notes that the participle for driven by the wind is the earliest known instance and was probably coined by the writer, who is fond of such verbs, and derives the last word from a bellows or fire-fan — the whole giving a picture of the sea whipped into white-caps and of a surface swaying restlessly under shifting breezes. Barnes draws the moral from the same image: a wave has no stability and lies at the mercy of every wind, and so a man who comes to God with unsettled convictions is driven about by each new feeling, hope and faith impelling him one moment and uncertainty filling him the next, so that the soul is as restless as the ocean. Wesley divides the two verbs neatly, that the man is driven with the wind from without and tossed from within by his own unstableness. Barnes adds the plain reason for the warning that follows: God sees the heart, and where there is no real trust in him it cannot be fitting that he should answer — which accounts for many a prayer that goes unanswered and many a return empty from the throne of grace.
8:
The adjective is a coinage, and Robertson makes something of that. It occurs here and once more in this letter and nowhere else that is known before it, so that the writer seems to have made the word himself, after which the early Christian writers copied it freely — which is one argument for an early date for the epistle. The sense is double-souled, or as Bunyan named the man, Facing-both-ways. Barnes gives the same derivation and its application, that the word describes one who is wavering and inconstant, a man with no settled principles who is controlled by passion and swayed by popular feeling, inclined now to one opinion and now to another. Wesley puts it in a line, that such a man has as it were two souls and his heart is not simply given up to God.

The phrase had a history among the Jews before it reached this letter. Clarke describes the man of two souls as having one for earth and one for heaven, wishing to secure both worlds, unwilling to give up the earth and loath to let heaven go; and he reports Rabbi Tanchum, commenting on Deuteronomy, that Scripture exhorts the Israelites when they pray not to have two hearts, one for the holy blessed God and one for something else. Clarke suspects a particular target, the Jews who were trying to incorporate the law with the gospel and were divided between them, unwilling to surrender the Levitical rites and unwilling to renounce the gospel; such men, he says, could make no progress in divine things. Ellicott would repunctuate, joining this verse to the last so that it reads as the reason why the doubter obtains nothing — he is a man of two minds and therefore uncertain in his ways — and takes the words for a proverb, matching the warning of Sirach not to come to God with a double heart. Gill fills out the picture from the other side: such a man halts between two opinions and cannot settle what to ask for, or else is not sincere in his requests but asks one thing while meaning another, drawing near with his mouth and honouring God with his lips while his heart is far from him.

What the last clause adds is a widening. Barnes points out that the instability is not confined to prayer, the matter actually in hand, but extends to everything: from the wavering shown in one thing the writer infers that firmness could be looked for in no other, and the man will be found irresolute in all. Barnes turns the observation round to make it useful, since a man who takes hold of the promises of God firmly and goes to him in every perplexity without hesitation will be found steady in his integrity and steadfast in his plans of life, a man whose character we understand and can confide in — such a man, he says, was Luther eminently. Calvin hears an implied contrast with what has gone before, between the simplicity of God, who gives with a stretched-out hand, and the double-mindedness of man, who ought in his turn to open the bosom of his heart; the unbelieving, having tortuous recesses in them, are never fixed, swelling one hour with the confidence of the flesh and sinking the next into despair. He notes that the word here means hesitation between faith and unbelief, faith being the subject, whereas in the fourth chapter it will mean hesitation between God and the world. Robertson glosses the second adjective as unsteady, fickle, staggering — reeling like a drunken man — and remarks that to this writer such doubt is plainly no mark of intellectuality.
9:
A new kind of trial is introduced, and Barnes names it: not affliction in general but the trial that comes with a change of circumstances, whether a man is raised from poverty to affluence or brought down from affluence to want. Wherever such a change occurs a man's religion is put to the test, and the poor man newly enriched should rejoice not in the means of gratification but because his faith is now being proved. There is hardly a more decisive trial, Barnes adds, since much religion that will bear poverty, and much that will bear prosperity, cannot bear the passage from one to the other — as many a frame can be seasoned to the heat of the equator or the cold of the north and yet cannot bear a rapid change between them. Robertson takes the lowly brother to be lowly in outward condition rather than in spirit, and observes that rich and poor in these churches already had their occasions of jealousy; the command that such a man glory in his high estate is a paradox and true, since in his low estate he stands at his height, the Cross being the great leveller. Gill notes that brother means one of the household of faith, and that the epithet describes not the temper of his mind but his outward state.

What the exaltation consists in is answered from his standing, not his prospects. Calvin sets the case beside Paul's word to servants, who were told to bear their lot as the freemen of God: the lowly are bidden to glory in having been adopted as God's children, and since it is beyond comparison the greatest dignity to be made the associate of Christ, a man who values that favour rightly will count everything else worthless, so that neither poverty nor contempt nor hunger will make him anxious. Clarke says the same in a sentence, that the destitute Christian may glory in the cross and the hope laid up for him, being an heir of God and a joint heir with Christ. Wesley notices that the title of brother is not given to the rich, and calls this rejoicing the most effectual remedy against double-mindedness. Ellicott guards the doctrine from a false humility: there is no praise here for the pride that apes lowliness or the affectation that loves to be despised, and if God is pleased to exalt the humble a magnificat should be sung anew — while for the finer spirits who shrink from any exaltation the apostle writes kindly, that they may not fear the greater dangers a higher call must bring.

What being made low means for the rich divides them. Barnes takes it plainly of losing his property, and observes that more Christians could bear that transition than the reverse; some of the loveliest exhibitions of piety he has seen were made in such a descent, new grace being given for the new trial as the most beautiful workings of the laws of matter appear in the chemist's rapid transitions. Calvin refuses that reading. He takes the particular for the general, so that the words touch everyone who excels in honour, and finds the lowness in the Christian state itself as the world estimates it, the kingdom of God teaching us to despise what we once admired. Against those who refer it to the stripping of the rich by persecution he objects from the context, since what follows speaks of the shortness of man's life rather than the fading of riches, the natural comfort had loss of property been meant. Ellicott sets the two states in antithesis, the rich man's humiliation against the poor man's humility, and hears a spiritual sense beneath it, teaching the poorest that he may be rich toward God — as the Spirit said to Smyrna, I know thy poverty, but thou art rich.
11:
What burns the grass is disputed in a small way. Gill keeps to the plain sense, taking it of the sun at midday, when it shines in full strength and its heat is scorching, especially in summer and in hot climates. Barnes points out that Isaiah, whom the writer plainly has in mind, names not the sun but a burning wind that dries up the flowers, and thinks the reference here is likewise to the fiery simoom which often rises with the sun and consumes the herbage. Robertson allows either: the noun is the word the Greek Old Testament gives to the sirocco, the dry east wind out of the desert, while elsewhere it means the burning heat of the sun, and both make sense here. He notes that the verbs state what always happens rather than what once happened, and that the flower is pictured as having a face, so that the grace which perishes is the beauty of its countenance. Clarke draws the physical cause out of it: the sun by its genial heat nourishes all plants, yet when it rises with a burning heat and the air holds too little moisture the juices are drawn out and the plant withers — so that the very cause of growth becomes the cause of decay.

Ellicott renders the whole in the past tense, the sun arose with the burning heat and dried up the grass, and the flower fell away and the grace of its fashion perished, taking the grace to be the loveliness and delicacy of its form, literally of its face. He supposes the writer had often watched the eastern sun scorching the verdure of the wilderness, with the cry of Isaiah in his ear that all flesh is grass, the flower fading while the word of God stands for ever. Barnes finds a further fitness once the stalk is brought in, since the hot wind withers the stalk that supports the flower and the flower falls when its support is gone — a man is blasted first, and the splendour that encircled him falls after him. Wesley remarks on the manner as much as the matter, finding an unspeakable beauty and elegance both in the comparison and in the way of expressing it, which intimates at once the certainty and the suddenness of the event.

The application to the rich man is where they differ. Barnes takes the phrase about his ways from Rosenmüller to mean his counsels and plans, so that the man vanishes with everything by which he was known; and since he must soon disappear with all his pomp, it is well that every change of condition should remind him, and he may rejoice in the providence that strips him and so tests his religion. Ellicott is careful about who is threatened: not the rich brother, though his wealth will pass away, but those that trust in riches, since the mammon of unrighteousness rightly used makes friends who receive us into everlasting habitations. He finds a special sharpness in the exact words, which mean that the rich shall perish in their journeyings after gain — a rebuke that could apply to no people more closely than to the Jews, the lenders unto many nations and the merchants of the world. Calvin is occupied with the text rather than the sense, preferring with Erasmus the reading without the diphthong, so that the phrase means in or with his riches rather than in his goings, though he grants that the received reading stands in far more copies. Clarke draws the practical lesson, that God gives and resumes these things at his pleasure, showing them uncertain so that they may never become an object of confidence; and that a man who suffers loss for righteousness' sake has gained what is of infinite worth and lost what he must soon have parted with.
12:
Gill takes the temptation to be affliction and the endurance to be a manner of bearing it: the man who so bears up under the weight as not to be offended at it, not to stumble in the ways of Christ and fall away from the truth as temporary believers do in a time of temptation, but stands manfully and does not sink. Such a man does not murmur or repine but is quiet and still, bears patiently and constantly, and endures to the end; he expects afflictions, and when they come he is not moved but continues in the work of the Lord. He is happy under his afflictions and even on account of them, since they are tokens of God's love and evidences of sonship. Henry sets the same point negatively: it is not every man who suffers that is blessed, but he who with patience and constancy goes through all difficulties in the way of duty, so that afflictions cannot make us miserable if it be not our own fault, and the tried Christian shall be a crowned one. Barnes takes the word in its widest sense, as anything that tries the reality of religion, whether affliction or a direct inducement to sin; and he answers why the chapter uses it two ways by observing that affliction is itself a solicitation, since under it the question comes whether we will hold to the religion for which we suffer or apostatise to escape it.

Clarke calls the saying a mere Jewish sentiment, and quotes the rabbinical parallel at length: blessed is the man who stands in his temptation, for there is no man whom God does not try; he tries the rich to see whether they will open their hands to the poor, and the poor to see whether they will receive affliction and not murmur, and to each who stands there is a double portion hereafter. This, he says, is exactly the sentiment before us, and he thinks the language borrowed from the Grecian contests, where he is crowned who conquers and none else. Ellicott hears rather the nine beatitudes of the mount, the words for endurance and trial being the very ones rendered patience and trials in the opening verses, and meaning steadfastness and tenacity of purpose. Robertson reads the participle as having become approved, pointing back to the testing named earlier, and takes the crown of life as a genitive of apposition — life itself being the crown, an honourable ornament rather than the victor's garland of leaves. Both he and Ellicott note that the word Lord is missing from the oldest manuscripts, Ellicott supposing a marginal gloss taken unwittingly into the text by a later copyist.

Calvin presses the paradox: they are not happy to whom all things come according to their wishes, but such as are not overcome with evils. The crown follows the contest, so that if our chief happiness is to be crowned in the kingdom of God it follows that the contests by which the Lord tries us are aids and helps to that happiness — an argument from the end. But they reason absurdly, he adds, who infer that we merit the crown by fighting, for God has gratuitously appointed it and our fighting only renders us fit to receive it; and love here is no more meritorious than the fighting, since God anticipates us by his own gratuitous love and the words only mark out the elect as those he approves. We lose courage in trial, on his account, for no other reason than that the love of the world prevails in us. Wesley makes the same connection in a line — his enduring proves his love, for it is love only that endureth all things — and Barnes observes how sufficiently the description distinguishes, since the great mass of men do not love God at all.
13:
The whole difficulty here is that one word has done two jobs, and Gill marks the turn plainly: up to this point temptations were matter of joy and boasting, the means of trying and exercising grace and of purging away the dross of corruption, temptations in which God was concerned; from here they are criminal, issuing in shame and death, to be deprecated and watched against, temptations to sin and in themselves sinful, which he removes and denies of God as unworthy of him. Clarke says the same more briefly, that lest the former sentiment should be misapplied the writer takes up the word in the sense of solicitation to sin after having used it of trial from providential circumstances, and so has explained and guarded his own meaning. Barnes reads the danger as real and pastoral rather than merely verbal: there was much in any trial that might induce a man to sin, whether by complaining, by murmuring, by apostasy or by yielding, and the perverse tendency of the heart would gladly charge that inducement on the God who arranged the trial. Whatever allurement a trial contains is incidental to it and no part of the divine purpose.

Robertson makes the point turn on a preposition. The construction expresses origin, not agency — the phrasing used elsewhere of Satan is different — so temptation does not spring from God at all; and he adds drily that contemptible as the excuse is, he has heard wicked and weak men blame God for their sins. The adjective that follows is a rare compound, the earliest example of its form, and Hort notes the phrase as a proverb meaning free from evils; Robertson grants that possible but insists the context calls for untemptable rather than untempted, since the clause that follows rests on it. Ellicott praises the old Geneva Bible here as the first of the versions to seize the exact meaning, where Wiclif, Tyndale and Cranmer had all missed it, and reads the sense as absolute: no possibility of temptation remains with God, into the splendour of his fulness no thought of wrong can enter, and it were blasphemy near to that of the Pharisees to think his kingdom so divided against itself that he should seduce his own subjects into revolt. Henry finds the ground of it in the divine nature, since all moral evil is owing to some want of wisdom or power or purity of will, and who can impeach the holy God with the want of what is his very essence?

Calvin distinguishes the two kinds carefully. External temptations are plainly sent by God, who tempted Abraham and daily tempts us by laying before us an occasion by which our hearts are made known; but to draw out what is hidden in a heart is a far different thing from inwardly alluring it by wicked lusts, and those flow from the corruption of our nature. He then raises the objection he knows is coming, that Scripture says men are blinded by God and given over to a reprobate mind, and answers that when it ascribes hardness of heart to God it assigns him neither the beginning of that blindness nor the blame of it: hearts are subjected to depraved lusts because they are already corrupt, and in giving them up God punishes sin rather than authors it. Barnes reaches the same conclusion by asking what could possibly move God — no evil passion to gratify, no want of power, no want of wealth, no want of happiness — and Henry adds that the evasion is hereditary, our first father having told God that the woman thou gavest me tempted me, and so in effect blamed God for giving him the tempter. Wesley leaves it at the bare denial, that God thus tempteth no man.
14:
Barnes is careful that the word for desire not be narrowed to libidinousness, as modern usage narrows it: it means desire in general, an earnest wish for anything, and seems here to cover the original propensities implanted in us as a stimulus to employment — the desire of knowledge, of food, of power. If there were no capacity for receiving food, objects appealing to the appetite could never tempt; if there were nothing in the soul that loved acquisition, gold would furnish no temptation. The propensity itself may be perfectly harmless; the fault is in not restraining the indulgence where we are commanded to, whether in the object sought or in the degree. Robertson finds the same double figure in the two participles, the first picturing a fish drawn out from his retreat and the second, from the noun for bait, meaning to catch fish by bait or to hunt with snares — allured by a definite lure, as Philo has it of pleasure. Clarke reads the two metaphors as dragging a fish out of the water by a hook concealed in a bait, and the enticements of an impure woman who draws the unwary into her snares; he thinks such connections are clearly in view, and quotes the rabbinical saying that evil concupiscence is at the beginning like the thread of a spider's web and afterwards like a cart rope.

Wesley marks the two stages against the two verbs: drawn away belongs to the beginning of the temptation, and means drawn out of God, our strong refuge; enticed belongs to its progress, catching at the bait. His conclusion is that we are to look for the cause of every sin in ourselves and not out of ourselves, since even the injections of the devil cannot hurt before we make them our own, and every man has desires arising from his own constitution, tempers, habits and way of life. Ellicott sets a limit to the tempter's power on the same ground: from without come the whispers of Satan, skilled in all that may entice, but the subtlest fiend can only guess what is passing in its victim's mind and shape its snares accordingly, since God alone is the discerner of hearts. So no power of hell can force the barriers the Holy Spirit erects around a faithful soul, and only by treason of the man himself can the enemy enter and reign. Calvin puts it shortly: since the inclination and excitement to sin are inward, in vain does the sinner seek a cause from an external impulse.

Gill traces the conceiving with some psychological patience — a proposal of pleasure or profit is made, agreeable to the principle of corrupt nature, and instead of resisting and rejecting the motion the man admits it, cherishes it, dallies with it, dwells upon it in his thoughts, hides it under his tongue as a sweet morsel, and contrives means to bring it about. Robertson takes each term in the birth vocabulary in turn, noting that the participle rendered full-grown means completeness of parts rather than maturity, the winged insect as against the grub, so that sin at birth is fully equipped for its career; and that the last verb is a medical word rather than a literary one, giving what he calls a powerful figure of abortion in which the child is dead at birth. Calvin warns against pressing the sequence into a doctrine, since it does not show when sin begins to be sin before God but only when it breaks forth; those who conclude that filthy lusts are no sins provided there is no assent have laid hold on the passage ignorantly. Ellicott lets the image stand as repellent, a hideous progeny tenfold more cursed than its begetter, and says the act itself is mortiferous as naturally as the work of poison on the body.
16:
The warning not to err is not a formality. Gill treats the error as fundamental: to make God the author of sin, or to charge him with being concerned in temptation to sin, strikes at his very being and at the perfection of his holiness, and is a denying of him, to be abhorred by all who profess any regard to his name. Barnes agrees the danger was real, since experience shows men are always prone to that opinion, and observes how the writer meets it — not by argument but by the opposite assertion, that so far from being the source of evil God is the author of all good. Ellicott marks the same hinge, that thus far the letter has declared what God is not and what qualities are alien to him, and now turns to the positive; the change from the dreadful tenor of the last verse to bright reflections on God's gifts is abrupt, and supplies a new incentive to endurance. Calvin calls it an argument from what is opposite: to do good is what properly belongs to God and accords with his nature, so whatever evil is done is not agreeable to it.

Two words are rendered by our one word gift, and the commentators make something of the distinction. Robertson takes the first as properly the act of giving and the second as the thing given, a benefaction, and thinks the contrast argues for giving as the sense of the first; he notes that the clause forms a perfect hexameter line, and that Ropes infers a quotation from an unknown source, though he does not find that conclusive. Ellicott, who calls the sentence more musical still in the Greek and likewise suspects the fragment of a Christian hymn, credits the Genevan version with observing the difference. On the lights themselves he refuses to choose among the readings on offer — figurative, or the mysterious Urim on Aaron's breast, or spiritual, or the material lights set in the firmament — and quotes Bishop Wordsworth's catalogue of all of them together, from the sun and stars to the light of reason and conscience and of the heavenly city. Cyril is drawn to the title itself, using the verse to insist that God did not attain in course of time to being a Father but is ever the Father of the Only-begotten, not by passion or union or effluence or alteration, since with him can be no variation. Wesley finds the appellation used with peculiar propriety just here, since it follows that he begat us.

The last clause turns on the very body it has just borrowed. Barnes draws the contrast out: the sun does not shine on all parts of the earth at once nor in the same manner all the year, but rises and sets, crosses the line and recrosses it, casting its light obliquely and producing the seasons; God is as if the sun stood in the meridian at noonday and never cast a shadow. Clarke adds eclipse and cloud to the figure, with the sun declining to the tropic of Capricorn and our days shortening in consequence, and draws the moral that men may hide from God's light by the works of darkness as owls and bats hide in caves while the sun shines. Robertson takes the two rare nouns in turn — the first an old word for making things alternate, used elsewhere of alternate stones in a pavement, the second a late word for a shade cast by one object on another — and admits the metaphor is unclear, whether the shadow on a dial or the moon's borrowed light lost behind the earth, and that the text itself is uncertain. Calvin's caution is the one that governs all of this: we may not measure the brightness of God by the irradiation of the sun which appears to us.
18:
Having said that every good gift comes down from above, the writer names one, and Gill thinks the instance well chosen: regeneration is the first gift of grace God bestows on his people openly and in their own persons, it involves the other gifts and prepares them for eternal life, and it is perfect because it is done at once. There are no degrees in it as there are in sanctification — a man is born again at once and born a perfect new man in all his parts, and no one is more regenerated than another, or the same person more at one time than at another. Barnes fastens on the participle: the fact that we are begotten to be his children is to be traced solely to his will, which purposed it and it was done. He is careful, though, not to let sovereign be read as arbitrary. It is not to be inferred that there was no reason why it should be done, only that his will determined the matter; there are good reasons in every case, though they are seldom stated to us and we might not comprehend them if they were. Robertson notes that the verb is the same one used a few lines earlier of lust bringing forth death, the metaphor of birth deliberately repeated in a good sense, and that it stands here of the father rather than the mother, which is very rare.

Clarke arranges the whole verse as a set of deliberate opposites to what has gone before: God's will against the lust of man, his truth as the means of salvation against the sinful means named above, and the new creature against the sin conceived and brought forth. Since the will of God is essentially good all its productions must be good, and since it is infinitely pure they must be holy. The instrument is the doctrine of truth, what Paul calls the word of the truth of the gospel, and Clarke adds a remarkable saying of Philo that God begat Isaac, sowing seed in souls and begetting happiness. Robertson takes the phrase as an instrumental case referring to the gospel message of salvation, a message marked by truth. Wesley calls it the true word, emphatically so termed. Ellicott hears a maternal phrase in the verb and lets it carry the tenderness: as the old creation was by the Word, so is the new, and though a woman may forget the son of her womb, he will never leave nor forsake.

What the firstfruits are is disputed, and the dispute is about how wide the harvest is. Clarke takes creatures to mean the Gentiles and firstfruits the Jews, to whom the gospel was first sent, those of them who believed being the firstfruits of the astonishing harvest God has since reaped over the whole Gentile world. Calvin notes that the qualifying word means in a manner or after a sort, and refuses to restrict the title to a few of the faithful, since as man excels among all creatures so the Lord elects some out of the whole mass and separates them as a holy offering; the firstfruits being a pledge of the coming harvest, creatures must include all the saved in future ages, and he too prefers the reading that makes the first converts, who were Jews, the firstfruits. Wesley enters one qualification, that the phrase is a kind of firstfruits because Christ alone is absolutely the firstfruits, Christians being the chief of God's visible creatures and sanctifying the rest. Ellicott reaches furthest, taking the words with Paul's groaning creation: every struggle animals make against pain and death shows these are a bondage imposed from without, so that every groan is an unconscious prophecy of liberation.
19:
Everything turns on what the wherefore looks back to. Gill takes it to the verse before — since the gospel, the word of truth, is the instrument God uses in regeneration and in forming a people for himself. Barnes spells the inference out: since God is the only source of good, since he tempts no man, and since by his sovereign goodness we have been made the firstfruits of his creatures, we ought to be ready to hear his voice and to bring our souls to entire practical obedience. Calvin agrees the exhortation is fitted to the subject in hand rather than a general sentence, and adds a reason for the urgency: spiritual generation is not the work of one moment, and since remnants of the old man abide in us we must be renewed through life, our own perverseness or arrogance or sloth being a great impediment to God in perfecting his work. Ellicott, who divides the chapter here into its third part, notes a small variation in the manuscripts that would make the opening not an address but a statement, ye know, my brethren beloved — and thinks the very abruptness of it may serve to arrest attention.

Robertson leaves that question where he finds it, saying only that the form can be either indicative or imperative and the context alone can decide. On the clauses he is precise: the picture points to listening to the word of truth just mentioned and is aimed against violent and disputatious speech, and the tense of the second means slow to begin speaking rather than slow while speaking; the third drops the infinitive, but probably means that slowness to speak up when angry will tend to curb the anger. Both Barnes and Clarke pile up the older sayings that anticipate the maxim. Clarke gives the rabbinical adage that the righteous speak little and do much while the wicked speak much and do nothing, and the son of Sirach's charge to be swift to hear and with deep consideration give answer. Barnes adds that men have two ears and but one tongue that they should hear more than they speak, that the ears are always open while the tongue is hedged in by a double row of teeth, and the reply of Xenocrates when asked why he alone kept silence — that he had sometimes had occasion to regret speaking, never that he was silent. Wesley reads the three clauses as a table of contents, the first treated from the next verse through the following chapter, the second in the third chapter, and the third through the fourth and fifth.

On wrath Henry makes the practical connection: if men would govern their tongues they must govern their passions, for when Moses' spirit was provoked he spoke unadvisedly with his lips. He applies it first to disputes among Christians, where each side should be willing to hear the other, people being often stiff in their opinions because they are unwilling to hear what can be offered against them; and he quotes Manton's report that when a Manichee contested with Augustine and cried importunately hear me, hear me, the father replied that neither should hear the other, but let both hear the apostle. Ellicott puts it in a phrase — the quick speaker is the quick kindler — and asks what we have to do with wrath at all, that a whole life should be wasted with such bitterness. Calvin takes the anger to be condemned specifically with regard to the hearing God demands, since making a tumult it disturbs and impedes him, and God cannot be heard except when the mind is calm and sedate. Barnes says the same of any inquiry after truth: a man whose mind is excited and enraged is in no condition to see the value of truth or to weigh the evidence for it.
20:
Robertson notices that the word for man here is the one opposed to woman rather than the inclusive term used a line earlier, and that the word for wrath means settled indignation rather than fury; so the saying does not deny that righteous indignation exists, only that a man is not necessarily promoting God's cause by his own personal anger. Barnes puts the same limit on the sense: it does not mean our wrath makes God more or less righteous, but that its tendency is not to produce the upright life he requires, and a man is never sure of doing right under excited feelings — he may do what is in the highest sense wrong and regret it all his life. Clarke will not leave it in the abstract. A furious zeal in religion is detestable in God's sight, who will have no sacrifice not consumed by fire from his own altar; the zeal that made the Papists persecute and burn the Protestants was kindled in hell, and worked no righteous act for God. Gill records the Alexandrian reading, which makes it an imperative — with the wrath of men do not work the righteousness of God — the practical point being that we should not attend on the word and ordinances with a wrathful spirit.

Gill hears in the next verse a boiling pot throwing up scum that must be taken off, the spirit of a wrathful man throwing up the filth of haughtiness and pride and anger, which must be laid aside or the word will not be heard to any profit. Robertson and Wesley both read the participle as a change of clothes, the verb being the ordinary one for putting off a garment and the first noun a late word meaning dirty — surely, says Robertson, a dirty garment. Wesley adds why the second noun calls wickedness superfluous: however necessary it may appear to worldly wisdom, every reasonable end may be answered without any degree of it. Ellicott observes that the word rendering it, nothingness in its derivation, was substituted in 1611 for the older and more correct malice, so that the badness implied in the original is much more positive than our version suggests; and he compares the overgrowth of evil to the thorns of the parable, which choke the good seed unless the rank crop is gathered and laid aside.

The last figure is disputed on a point of vocabulary. Barnes takes it as engrafting, an art everywhere known, and draws comfort from it: however crabbed our nature, or however bitter the fruit it would bear of itself, through the implanted word it may produce the fruits of righteousness. Clarke applies the image historically: the Jews had been planted by God as a right vine, and when they received the gospel it was engrafted on that good stock, the pure knowledge of the true God and his moral law. Robertson objects that the adjective is not the word for engrafted at all but a verbal from the verb to grow in, meaning properly ingrown or inborn — the rooted word, sown in the heart as the soil or garden of God. Calvin reaches nearly the same sense from the requirement rather than the etymology: the word cannot be rightly received unless it strikes roots in us, for seed sown on hard ground soon withers. He takes the meekness to be humility and a mind ready to learn, and thinks so few profit in God's school because hardly one in a hundred renounces the stubbornness of his own spirit. And when the word is called able to save, he adds the necessary guard: the power of saving is not ascribed to the external sound, nor is the office of saving taken from God and transferred elsewhere, for the word meant is the one that penetrates the heart by faith.
22:
Calvin heads off the obvious objection first: the doer meant here is not the doer who satisfies the law in every part, but the man who from the heart embraces God's word and testifies by his life that he really believes it — blessed are they that hear God's word and keep it. The fruits show what that implanting was, and faith is not excluded but included especially, as the chief work God requires. Gill fills the description out likewise: the doers are those who spiritually understand the word, gladly receive it, obey it from the heart, submit to the ordinances it directs them to, and walk becoming their profession. Clarke names the disease instead. They had heard the doctrine and believed it and put it to no practical use; they were downright Antinomians who put a stupid, inactive faith in the place of all moral righteousness, and had reasoned themselves into carnal security. Robertson takes the verb as continuous — keep on becoming doers — and translates the participle from its parts, to reckon aside and so wrongly: such a man deludes nobody but himself.

Barnes puts his finger on what exactly the deception consists in. It is the imagination that hearing is all that is required, so that a man who supposes his punctual attendance on preaching has done all that is demanded of him is under a gross self-deception; and multitudes are utterly regardless of the word's claims to obedience once the hearing is over. Henry states it as sharply: if we heard a sermon every day, and an angel from heaven were the preacher, resting in the hearing only would never bring us to heaven. Mere hearers are self-deceivers, and self-deceit will be found the worst deceit at last; if we flatter ourselves it is our own fault, for the truth flatters no man. Ellicott finds a play in the Greek our language cannot supply, the word for deceiving being the contrary of the word for the message and meaning its corruption — what is the source of knowledge and life can be so handled as to cause error and death. The danger, he adds, is subtler than hypocrisy: a man may be blind and nevertheless exclaim that he sees.

The mirror was not glass. Robertson notes that ancient mirrors were polished metal, of silver or usually of copper and tin, and Ellicott adds that such mirrors are still used in the East; the face seen in one is literally the face of a man's birth, the real appearance the word of God properly looked into will afford him. Clarke works the comparison out at length, and it is the best thing in his note: a man looks in the mirror, sees deformities that might be remedied, is affected by the sight and forms purposes of improvement — then goes away, the mirror is removed, his face is no longer reflected to him, and he forgets both how disagreeable he appeared and what he resolved. The doctrines of God faithfully preached are such a mirror, and when the preaching is over the mirror is taken away. Robertson insists the tenses be read as they stand rather than as timeless: he glanced at himself, and off he has gone, and straightway forgot what sort of man he was. Ellicott likewise takes it as an actual occurrence the writer had seen, the recognition of a well-known face followed by instant and complete forgetfulness. Calvin's summary is shortest: heavenly doctrine is a mirror in which God presents himself to our view, but what is spoken of here is the external glance of the eye and not the meditation that penetrates the heart, and a doctrine merely heard avails nothing because it soon vanishes. Wesley marvels how exactly the scripture glass shows a man the face of his soul, and warns that such forgetting does not excuse.
25:
The verb rendered looketh into is unusually vivid, and the commentators disagree about how much weight it will bear. Clarke calls it very emphatic, signifying the deep and attentive consideration given to something a man cannot bring up to his eyes, so that he must bend his back and neck and stoop down to see it to advantage; and he takes the metaphor from women who spend much time at the glass, that not one hair or the smallest ornament may be left out of place. Wesley reads it the same way — not with a transient glance, but bending down, fixing his eyes, and searching all to the bottom. Robertson is more cautious: the notion of stooping is not strong here, and Hort shows the word can mean only a cursory glance, though the contrast with the previous verse seems to preclude that sense. Barnes goes further and denies the contrast lies there at all. The word used of the careless man also implies intense observation, so the point is not the manner of looking but the duty of continuing; the emphasis falls on persevering in the observance rather than on how closely a man peers.

Gill argues at some length that the law meant is not the moral law but the gospel, since that is what the context has been speaking of — the word of truth by which God begets men, the implanted word able to save, the thing men are to be doers of; and he thinks it called a law not strictly, as a code of precepts enforced by penalties, but in the Jewish sense of teaching or instruction, since it is a declaration of righteousness by Christ and a free promise of eternal life. Calvin complains that interpreters have not understood why it is called perfect and of liberty, for want of noticing a contrast: as long as the law is preached by the external voice of man and not inscribed by the Spirit on the heart it is a dead letter, and so imperfect and a law of bondage; but the Spirit of regeneration who writes it inwardly brings the grace of adoption with it, and freedom from fear follows the adoption inseparably. Robertson likewise takes the liberty to rest on the work of Christ, whose truth sets us free, and Ellicott quotes Alford to the same effect — the phrase is not set against a former law of bondage but describes the law of the new life and birth, with its spontaneous and free development of obedience.

Clarke hears behind the warning about forgetting the charge in Deuteronomy to keep the soul diligently lest a man forget the things his eyes have seen, and adds the rabbinical saying that he who studies and forgets is like a woman who brings forth children and immediately buries them. He gives too the fourfold classification of those who visit the synagogue: he who enters but does not work, he who works but does not enter, he who does both, and he who does neither — the first two indifferent, the third the righteous man, the fourth wholly evil. Ellicott renders the balanced phrase literally, not a hearer of forgetfulness but a doer of work, and says comment is needless once it is put so; he hears in the closing blessing a return to the beatitudes and the end of the sermon on the mount, this humbly active Christian being the wise man who built his house upon a rock. Barnes takes the promise as made to the act itself: a man is blessed in the very keeping, which produces peace of conscience and imparts happiness of a high order. Calvin says the same in fewer words — blessedness is to be found in doing, not in cold hearing.
26:
Ellicott reads the turn structurally: having dilated so far on the first part of the earlier advice, be swift to hear, the writer now enforces the second, be slow to speak. He also presses the verb rendered seem, which the English obscures — it means seem to himself, not merely to others, so the warning is aimed not at the hypocrite but at the self-deceived. A Christian can hardly help feeling that he is a religious man, and so far well; the danger is that he may give proof of his self-delusion by not curbing his tongue. Gill takes the appearance to rest on preaching or praying or hearing and the other external duties a man is constant in, and notes that several versions render the clause as thinking himself religious. Robertson takes the sense of the adjective from Hatch, who shows it refers to the external observances of public worship — church attendance, almsgiving, prayer, fasting — the Pharisaic element in Christian worship; the word itself is of uncertain etymology and is found nowhere else outside lexicons. Clarke reports the guess of Suidas, that Orpheus the Thracian instituted the religious rites of the Greeks and the verb for worship was named as a Thracian invention.

Barnes makes the argument turn on a principle: religion is designed to bring the whole man under control, so if there is any one propensity it does not govern, that single exception proves the seat of the evil has never been reached. A man may have zeal, outward benevolence, an uncommon gift in prayer, much self-denial as with those who withdraw into monasteries, even deep conviction of sin and great joy at his supposed conversion, and one unrestrained sin will neutralise all of it. Robertson observes that the compound verb here is the earliest known example of its form and that the picture is precise: a man putting the bridle in his own mouth, not in another's. Wesley specifies what the tongue is to be bridled from — backbiting, talebearing, evilspeaking — and says the man who does not so bridle it only deceives his own heart if he fancies he has any true religion at all. Ellicott makes gentleness of tongue the first mark of true religion, as blasphemy is the most damning fault, but warns that the text is a guide for self-examination rather than a stone to cast at a neighbour, and sends the reader to Bishop Butler's sermon on the government of the tongue.

Calvin identifies the particular sin more narrowly as detraction, and explains why it belongs just here. Those who have put off the grosser vices are especially subject to it: a man who is neither adulterer nor thief nor drunkard, but seems brilliant with some outward show of sanctity, will set himself off by defaming others under pretence of zeal. And he traces the slander to its root in self-flattery, quoting Aesop's fable that the wallet hanging behind is not seen — men blinded by immoderate love of themselves believe themselves far better than they are, and would forgive readily if they in turn acknowledged their own need of forgiveness. Henry states the connection flatly: the man who has a slandering tongue cannot have a truly humble, gracious heart, and readiness to speak of the faults of others, or to lessen their wisdom and piety, is a sign of vain religion. Clarke turns it upon teachers in particular. No matter where a man has studied, if he has not learned religion he can never teach it, since religion is learned only by experience; and his advice to such a one is blunt — if he is old let him retire to the desert and pray for light, if in the prime of life let him turn to some honest calling, and if he is young let him tarry at Jericho till his beard grows.
27:
Gill takes pure and undefiled to mean simply sincere and genuine, free from adulteration and hypocrisy. Ellicott presses a point that matters for the whole verse: what is meant is religious service, and no single English word will carry that sense, so religion in its ordinary meaning misleads — real worship, beheld and acknowledged as such in the presence of God, is what is described. Robertson agrees, citing examples in the papyri and inscriptions of the word used for ritual and reverential worship under the empire, and quotes Hort's caution that this is not a definition of religious worship at all but a pertinent illustration of the spirit that leads to such acts. Calvin makes the same reservation with an illustration of his own: when a man given to wine and gluttony boasts that he is temperate, and another objects that the temperate man is he who does not indulge in excess, the object is not to express the whole of temperance but to name one thing suitable to the subject in hand. What is being said is that religion without these things is nothing, and that it is not to be estimated by the pomp of ceremonies.

Barnes states the limit plainly — the apostle does not say this is the whole of religion, or that nothing else is essential — and then reduces the two specimens to their principles: religion will lead to a life of practical benevolence, and it will keep us unspotted from the world. If a man is truly benevolent he bears the image of the God who is the fountain of benevolence; if his walk is uncontaminated he resembles his Maker, for God is holy. Both Barnes and Clarke report the suggestion that the two adjectives are borrowed from gems, whose perfection lies in being free from flaws, not cloudy but of a pure water; Barnes credits it to Rosenmüller. Clarke then digresses into the etymology of our own word religion, giving Cicero's derivation from re and lego, of those not satisfied with what was commonly said of the gods but reading the matter through again, and Lactantius's rejoinder that it comes rather from the bond of piety which binds us to God — a bond Lucretius laboured to dissolve when he undertook to loose men from religion's chains. Robertson notes only that the second adjective puts negatively what the first says positively.

On the visiting itself Clarke is at his most insistent. The verb means to take oversight of, so true religion does not merely give something for the relief of the distressed but visits them, takes them under its care, goes to their houses and speaks to their hearts, relieves their wants, instructs them in divine things and recommends them to God; and he turns on the reader to ask whether his religion has ever led him to cellars and garrets to find out the distressed. Wesley makes the same threefold division of the visit — counsel, comfort and relief — to those who need it most, in their most helpless and hopeless state; but he adds that neither this nor the keeping unspotted can be done till we have given our hearts to God and love our neighbour as ourselves. Calvin reads the orphans and widows as a part standing for the whole, so that under one particular the writer recommends every act of love. Ellicott takes the two requirements as a double proof of one life, and observes how often the help afforded to the helpless will itself bring about the unworldliness; he ends with a caution against cold reliance upon ritual, remembering the scrupulous contemporaries who would not enter the judgment hall lest they be defiled while they sought to slay the one who had told them that what comes out of a man is what defiles him.
